name: Bañados-Teitelboim-Zanelli Black Hole
description: A rotating black hole in three spacetime dimensions with a negative cosmological constant. It has constant negative curvature everywhere, being anti-de Sitter space with points identified by a discrete boost, and it carries a temperature and an entropy that can be computed exactly.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, with $M = 8Gm/c^2$ and $J = 8Gj/c^3$ for a hole of mass $m$ and angular momentum $j$, and $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions. We write $N^2 = r^2/\ell^2 - M + J^2/(4r^2)$, which vanishes on the horizons $r_\pm^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}M\ell^2\left(1 \pm \sqrt{1 - J^2/(M^2\ell^2)}\right)$.
history: In three spacetime dimensions gravity has no local degrees of freedom outside its sources: Stanley Deser, Roman Jackiw, and Gerard 't Hooft showed in 1984 that every region free of sources is flat, and that a localized source changes the geometry only globally [deser1984]. With a cosmological constant the curvature outside the sources is constant, as Deser and Jackiw found the same year, so that with a negative one empty space is locally anti-de Sitter space everywhere [deser1984cosmological]. Máximo Bañados, Claudio Teitelboim (now Claudio Bunster), and Jorge Zanelli found in 1992 that the theory with a negative cosmological constant $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$ has a black hole [banados1992]. Its metric carries a mass $M$ and an angular momentum $J$, with an outer and an inner horizon at $r_\pm^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}M\ell^2\left(1 \pm \sqrt{1 - J^2/(M^2\ell^2)}\right)$ for $M > 0$ and $|J| \le M\ell$ [banados1992]. For $-1 < M < 0$ the solutions carry naked conical singularities, which they excluded from the physical spectrum; at $M = -1$ and $J = 0$ the singularity disappears and anti-de Sitter space emerges as a "bound state," separated "from the continuous black hole spectrum by a mass gap of one unit" [banados1992].¶Bañados, Teitelboim, and Zanelli found the entropy of the hole "equal to twice the perimeter length of the horizon," $S = 4\pi r_+$ in their units, $8G = \hbar = 1$, which is the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy $2\pi r_+/(4G\hbar)$ with the length of the horizon in place of its area [banados1992]. The outer horizon has surface gravity $\kappa = (r_+^2 - r_-^2)/(\ell^2r_+)$, which sets the Hawking temperature $T = \hbar c\,\kappa/(2\pi k_B)$ [banados1992]. The temperature is zero for the extreme hole, $|J| = M\ell$, whose entropy stays nonzero [banados1992]. The curvature is the same at every point, $R = -6/\ell^2$, and the Kretschmann scalar is $12/\ell^4$ [banados1992].¶Bañados, Marc Henneaux, Teitelboim, and Zanelli showed in 1993 that the black hole is anti-de Sitter space with its points identified by a discrete subgroup of its isometry group $SO(2,2)$, so it is locally anti-de Sitter space everywhere [banados1993]. The curvature is finite at $r = 0$, and $r = 0$ is "a singularity in the causal structure": continued past it, the spacetime would hold closed timelike curves [banados1993]. They gave Kruskal coordinates and drew the Penrose diagrams of the static and the rotating hole, and showed that coupling matter to the hole puts a curvature singularity at $r = 0$ [banados1993]. The hole of zero mass, whose horizons have shrunk to $r = 0$, "differs from anti-de Sitter space and plays the role of the vacuum" [banados1993]. Pressureless dust collapsing under a negative cosmological constant ends as the stationary black hole of Bañados, Teitelboim, and Zanelli, as Robert Mann and Simon Ross found in 1993 [mann1993]. Gary Horowitz and Dean Welch made the hole an exact solution of string theory that year by adding an antisymmetric tensor field proportional to the volume form, which turns it into the orbifold of the Wess-Zumino-Witten model on $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ that describes strings on anti-de Sitter space [horowitz1993].¶J. David Brown and Marc Henneaux had shown in 1986 that, with suitable boundary conditions, the symmetries of three dimensional gravity with a negative cosmological constant at infinity form the conformal group of two dimensions, with a central charge that is "just the Virasoro central charge" [brown1986]. Andrew Strominger put that central charge, $c = 3\ell/(2G)$, into John Cardy's formula for the growth of the number of states of a conformal field theory, and in 1998 found the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of the hole exactly [cardy1986, strominger1998]. The same count applies to black holes whose geometry near the horizon is locally that of three dimensional anti-de Sitter space, among them black holes of string theory in five dimensions whose geometry near the horizon is a Bañados-Teitelboim-Zanelli hole [strominger1998]. Juan Maldacena and Strominger showed in 1998 that identifying the points of anti-de Sitter space produces a density matrix whose temperature and entropy are the hole's [maldacena1998stringy].¶The frequencies at which a perturbed hole rings down coincide exactly with the poles of the retarded correlation function of the same perturbation in the dual conformal field theory, as Danny Birmingham, Ivo Sachs, and Sergey Solodukhin found in 2002 [birmingham2002]. Edward Witten proposed in 2007 that pure gravity in three dimensions with a negative cosmological constant is dual to an extremal conformal field theory, which "at the most negative possible value of the cosmological constant" is very likely the monster theory of Igor Frenkel, James Lepowsky, and Arne Meurman [witten2007]. Alexander Maloney and Witten summed the contributions of the known classical geometries, these black holes among them, to the partition function exactly, and found the result "not physically sensible": at one energy it counts $-6$ states [maloney2010].

related.text: The rotating black hole of four dimensions. The BTZ black hole has an outer and an inner horizon as Kerr's does, in a spacetime of constant curvature [banados1992].
The black hole of anti-de Sitter space in four dimensions, which has a curvature singularity at its centre.

The BTZ black hole is anti-de Sitter space of three dimensions with its points identified, so it is locally anti-de Sitter space everywhere. At $M = -1$ and $J = 0$ it is anti-de Sitter space [banados1992, banados1993].
Minkowski space identified under a boost, as the BTZ black hole is anti-de Sitter space identified under one [misner1967, banados1993].

Sören Holst and Hans-Jürgen Matschull showed in 1999 that two massless particles colliding in anti-de Sitter space make a Gott universe, which, with its closed timelike curves treated as singular, is a rotating BTZ black hole [holst1999].

The spinning point particle of gravity in three dimensions with no cosmological constant, drawn out along a line into a string. It has no horizon, and its closed timelike curves lie close to the source [deser1984, deser1992time].
The rotating black hole of anti-de Sitter space in four dimensions. Its boundary is a rotating Einstein universe too, one dimension up [hawking1999rotation].

Schwarzschild's metric with a constant $\lambda^2$ added to $-g_{tt}$, a wormhole that passes for a black hole. Sergey Solodukhin made that change first in the BTZ black hole, in 2005, to restore unitarity [solodukhin2005, damour2007].

Dust collapsing to a black hole in four dimensions. Robert Mann and Simon Ross carried the collapse over to three in 1993, where dust falling under a negative cosmological constant ends as a BTZ black hole [mann1993].
The same identification of points carried to four dimensions, where the horizon comes out a torus or a surface of genus two or more [aminneborg1996].
A black hole in two dimensions, found in string theory. Times a circle, it is the string dual of the BTZ hole without rotation [horowitz1993].

With no cosmological constant a mass in three dimensions makes a cone and no black hole. Hans-Jürgen Matschull collided two such particles in anti-de Sitter space in 1999 and got this black hole [deser1984, matschull1999].

coordinates.name: Stationary

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$
Mass, dimensionless, $M = 8Gm/c^2$ for a hole of mass $m$, with $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions
Angular momentum, a length, $J = 8Gj/c^3$ for a hole of angular momentum $j$; a horizon exists only for $|J| \le M\ell$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$
Mass, dimensionless, $M = 8Gm/c^2$ for a hole of mass $m$, with $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions
Angular momentum, a length, $J = 8Gj/c^3$ for a hole of angular momentum $j$; a horizon exists only for $|J| \le M\ell$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \tilde\phi)$, with the advanced time $v$ a length, $dv = c\,dt + dr/N^2$ and $d\tilde\phi = d\phi + J\,dr/(2r^2N^2)$.

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$
Mass, dimensionless, $M = 8Gm/c^2$ for a hole of mass $m$, with $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions
Angular momentum, a length, $J = 8Gj/c^3$ for a hole of angular momentum $j$; a horizon exists only for $|J| \le M\ell$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \tilde\phi)$, with the retarded time $u$ a length, $du = c\,dt - dr/N^2$ and $d\tilde\phi = d\phi - J\,dr/(2r^2N^2)$.
